name: Nirvana fallacy
statement: The nirvana fallacy rejects a workable option by measuring it against an unattainable ideal instead of against the alternatives actually available.
meaning: The move has three parts. An option is on the table, a standard is produced that nothing available can reach, and the gap between them is treated as a reason to refuse. What makes it a fallacy is the comparison class. A choice is made among the things that can be had, so a standard none of them meets cannot rank them. Harold Demsetz's version is narrower than the popular one. He was writing about how economists judge institutions, and his complaint was that a demonstrated gap between a market and a perfect market was being read as proof that the market had failed. The popular version drops the institutions and keeps the shape, so that any argument running 'this does not solve the whole problem, so do not do it' gets the name. Neither version claims anything about how often people reason this way. Demsetz offered no data and reported no study. The nirvana fallacy is therefore a charge about an argument rather than a measured tendency, which is why the entries in this atlas that carry numbers describe narrower behaviour than the fallacy does.

origin.where: The Journal of Law and Economics
origin.note: The article is 'Information and Efficiency: Another Viewpoint', volume 12, pages 1 to 22, written at the University of Chicago and framed as a critique of Kenneth Arrow's 1962 paper on the allocation of resources for invention. Demsetz names the target on his first page: 'This nirvana approach differs considerably from a comparative institution approach in which the relevant choice is between alternative real institutional arrangements.' He writes 'nirvana approach' seven times, 'nirvana viewpoint' once and 'nirvana view' twice. The phrase 'nirvana fallacy' occurs nowhere in the article, which was read in full from the scanned JSTOR copy at the URL given and checked again in a partial reprint. The name in general use is later than the paper and its coiner was not identified here.

evidence: Demsetz's argument is about method in policy economics, and every example in it is an argument rather than a person. He sets out the contrast in his opening paragraph: those who adopt the nirvana viewpoint 'seek to discover discrepancies between the ideal and the real and if discrepancies are found, they deduce that the real is inefficient', while users of the comparative institution approach 'attempt to assess which alternative real institutional arrangement seems best able to cope with the economic problem'. A footnote closes the obvious escape. 'A practitioner of the nirvana approach sometimes discusses and compares alternative institutional arrangements. But if all are found wanting in comparison with the ideal, all are judged to be inefficient.' He then names three errors the approach invites: the grass is always greener fallacy, the fallacy of the free lunch, and the people could be different fallacy. The first is invoking an unexamined alternative, and he illustrates it with Arrow's conclusion that optimal allocation to invention 'would be necessary for the government or some other agency not governed by profit-and-loss criteria to finance research and invention', which Demsetz restates as the claim that removing the nonoptimalities would remove the nonoptimalities. The second is treating a gap as a loss without costing the fix, and he applies it to Arrow's treatment of missing commodity-option markets: if such markets are costly to run, their absence is not a demonstration of inefficiency, and to say otherwise 'is to deny that scarcity is relevant to optimality'. The third is reaching an ideal by assuming different people, which he pins on Arrow's handling of moral hazard in insurance. His closing section gives the general form. To call private enterprise inefficient because indivisibilities, costly knowledge, moral hazard and risk aversion exist 'is to say little more than that the competitive equilibrium would be different if these were not the facts of life'. Nothing in the paper is an experiment, and the same holds for the literature that adopted the name. What has been measured sits in narrower places. The zero-risk bias entry records the choice of clearing one hazard completely over a larger cut in total harm, and the omission bias entry records the asymmetry between harm caused and harm allowed, including the vaccination studies. A third measured construct comes closest to the medical case and is still not this one. Abdelaziz Alsharawy, Esha Dwibedi, Jason Aimone and Sheryl Ball ran a preregistered vignette experiment with 888 United States residents on Amazon Mechanical Turk in March 2021. The unvaccinated faced a stated 2 per cent risk of death and the vaccinated 1.01 per cent, of which 1 per cent came from the virus. Only the description of the remaining 0.01 per cent changed. Called problems unrelated to the vaccine it was a control; called vaccine-induced complications it was betrayal. Willingness to vaccinate fell by 0.453 points on a seven-point scale, Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 0.001, and 8.4 per cent more respondents crossed into the hesitant category, McNemar p < 0.001. More than 30 per cent of respondents showed a positive level of betrayal aversion. Attributing the same 0.01 per cent to government or to scientists produced larger effects than side effects did, p < 0.010. A regret message raised willingness and cut hesitancy by about 11.7 per cent, one-sided Fisher's exact p = 0.032, and left betrayal aversion where it was. The total risk was held constant across conditions, so what those participants rejected was a source of harm and not a shortfall against an ideal.

replication.headline: No experiment on the nirvana fallacy was found. Searches returned law, economics and policy essays that use the name and no psychology that tests it.
replication.detail: The search covered Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex and general web search, in each case for 'nirvana fallacy' and 'perfect solution fallacy', plus targeted searches for preregistered work on OSF and PsyArXiv. Crossref's fifteen closest matches for the first phrase are essays on antitrust, fair use, corporate governance, failed states, artificial intelligence and bioethics. OpenAlex returned 381 records, and the twenty-five ranked most relevant sit in law, economics, public policy and bioethics. PubMed holds two records containing the phrase, a 2013 commentary in The American Journal of Bioethics and a 2019 article in Science and Engineering Ethics, neither of them a study of reasoning. 'Perfect solution fallacy' returned nothing in PubMed and nothing on point in Crossref. Nine PubMed records combine 'perfect enemy of the good' with decision making and all nine are editorials or commentary. Semantic Scholar was queried and returned a rate-limit error rather than results, so that index was not covered. No paper was found in which participants are shown an argument of this shape and asked to judge it, and none in which an experimenter varies whether a rejected option is compared with an ideal or with the alternatives on offer. The state is none-located because a search was made and came up empty, not because the fallacy has been tested and survived or failed.

limits: The idea has no measured content of its own, so most of what a reader wants from this page is held by other entries. Zero-risk bias and omission bias carry the experimental record for refusing a real option that leaves some harm in place, and neither of them supports the nirvana fallacy as stated, because neither varies the comparison standard. Koehler and Gershoff's 2003 safety-product studies are quoted here only through Alsharawy and colleagues, who describe them as finding participants more likely to buy airbags and smoke alarms, and marginally more likely to take vaccines, when the residual risk involved no betrayal. That paper's full text was not obtained and no figure from it is quoted. Alsharawy and colleagues run a single hypothetical disease on one online panel in one country in one month, and their design holds total risk constant, which is what makes it clean and also what puts it beside this entry rather than inside it. Demsetz is a normative argument in economics and cannot be right or wrong in the way an effect can. Whether his charge lands against Arrow is a question this page does not settle, and the replies to it in the market-failure literature were not read. The Arrow passages quoted above are quoted as Demsetz prints them; Arrow's own chapter was not obtained.
misreadings: The commonest error is that Demsetz coined the phrase. He did not write it. The excerpt of the article circulated by the Collegium Institute carries an editors' headnote saying 'Demsetz calls this the "nirvana fallacy", a term he coined in this article', and the phrase appears in that headnote and nowhere in the twenty-two pages it introduces. The second error is treating Voltaire as the source. La Bégueule of 1772 opens 'Dans ses écrits un sage Italien / Dit que le mieux est l'ennemi du bien', which credits an Italian writer rather than claiming the line, and a proverb about perfectionism is not the same object as a claim about comparison classes. The third error is losing the politics. Demsetz aimed the charge at the case for government intervention, and his own preferred conclusion was that private arrangements are being judged against a standard no arrangement can meet. The name is now used in both directions, which is fair, and it means quoting Demsetz for a general-purpose fallacy quotes him for something wider than he wrote. The fourth error is folding it into neighbouring moves. A false dilemma prunes the options; the nirvana fallacy leaves the options alone and imports a standard that none of them meets. Moving the goalposts raises a standard after evidence has met it, which needs a first standard and a change of mind, neither of which this move requires. The fifth error is the one this atlas is most likely to be asked to make, which is to read the zero-risk bias experiments as measurements of this fallacy. Those studies vary how a fixed effort is divided across two hazards, and no ideal appears in the problem. The sixth error is thinking the label settles anything. Calling an argument a nirvana fallacy asserts that the standard invoked is out of reach, and where the ideal is in fact attainable the charge is simply false.

sources.text: Demsetz, H. (1969). Information and efficiency: Another viewpoint. The Journal of Law and Economics, 12(1), 1-22. Read in full from the scanned JSTOR copy hosted by Texas A&M University; every quotation was re-extracted from the document text.

Collegium Institute. Information and efficiency: Another viewpoint (in part). A partial reprint with an editors' headnote. Used here as a second reading of the quoted passages and as the source of the claim that Demsetz coined the phrase 'nirvana fallacy' in the article.
Voltaire. (1772). La Bégueule: Conte moral. Opening couplet read at French Wikisource; it attributes 'le mieux est l'ennemi du bien' to an unnamed Italian writer.
